analysis.one_liner: Taxes fund managers' carried-interest profits at normal income rates instead of lower investment rates.
analysis.headline: The bill to end the carried interest tax break was introduced in May 2021 with 14 Senate sponsors and never received a hearing, a vote, or any action in the Senate Finance Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Managers of private equity, hedge fund, and real estate partnerships take much of their pay as a share of fund profits, called carried interest. Under current law that pay is taxed at the lower rate for investment gains, up to 20%, rather than as regular income at up to 37%. This bill would tax that pay as ordinary income, treat it as self-employment income subject to payroll taxes, and raise the penalty to 40% for tax underpayments tied to avoiding the rule.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly: closing the loophole raises federal revenue from a small group of very high earners, money that would otherwise come from other taxpayers or be added to deficits. Fund managers themselves would pay tens of thousands to millions more in taxes each year.

how_it_helps.text: The bill treats the net capital gain from an investment services partnership interest as ordinary income, ending the lower capital-gains rate on compensation paid as a share of fund profits [S2].

It also counts income from these interests as self-employment income for payroll tax purposes [S2], and imposes a doubled, 40% penalty on tax underpayments from failing to treat this income correctly [S2] [S3].
It closes related routes around the rule, including partnership interests transferred for services, SPAC sponsor gains, and publicly traded partnership treatment [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Executives and partners at private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, and real estate investment partnerships, whose compensation would be taxed at the top ordinary income rate plus payroll taxes. Their firms might also face higher costs or restructure compensation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: Supporters of current treatment argue that fund managers take long-term investment risk alongside investors, so their share of profits is genuinely investment income, and that taxing it as wages could discourage the risk capital that funds startups, businesses, and rental housing. The bill itself acknowledges the scale of the change, with special rules separating true invested capital from compensation so that only the service-linked portion is taxed [S3].
The bill carves out certain family partnerships from the stricter allocation rules [S2], a narrower break than the general rule and the kind of exception that reduces revenue and adds complexity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is straightforward tax fairness: compensation for managing other people's money is taxed like work rather than like a stock sale. The main cost is that some fund managers would restructure compensation or invest less, and the transition rules would not touch existing gains already accrued. The family-partnership carve-out is a real, if limited, hole. On balance, the revenue and simplicity of taxing this pay like wages outweighs the transition cost for people who do not work in fund management.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2021 and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced the Carried Interest Fairness Act of 2021 on May 12, 2021, joined by 13 cosponsors including Sen. Manchin, Sen. Brown, Sen. Warren, and Sen. Sanders [S1] [S3] [S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a committee hearing or vote and never reached the Senate floor before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
All 14 Senate sponsors were Democrats or allied Independents — 12 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Independents — and no Republican sponsored the bill [S3] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate fund managers are better off: the carried interest tax break they receive stayed in place because the bill never advanced, while other taxpayers continued to bear the federal revenue gap it would have closed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fund managers keeping the tax break

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors were Democrats or allied Independents; no Republican sponsored the bill, and it never came to a vote that would have shown the broader split [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: The bill converts their main form of compensation, carried interest, from the 20% capital gains rate to ordinary income rates up to 37% and subjects it to payroll taxes. Their interest in keeping the current break runs against ordinary taxpayers, who otherwise make up the revenue.
Rental and investment real estate counts as a specified asset, so real estate fund sponsors' profit shares would also be taxed as ordinary income.
The bill explicitly applies to SPAC sponsor interests and investment entities, closing routes around the capital-gains treatment.
